claims.label: No organism self-fertilises indefinitely; occasional crosses are needed
claims.statement: It is a general law of nature that no organism fertilises itself for an unlimited number of generations; an occasional cross with another individual, perhaps at long intervals, is indispensable, even in hermaphrodites.

operationalizations.text: Use population genomic linkage disequilibrium, heterozygosity, and coalescent analyses across obligately selfing hermaphrodites and asexual lineages to test whether any lineages persist over geological timescales ('an eternity of generations') without any outcrossing or genetic exchange, and compare extinction rates of strict selfers against outcrossers.

Identify lineages with genomic evidence of prolonged obligate selfing and test persistence, fertility and genetic load through time. Any indefinitely selfing, persistent lineage would refute the universal claim, while recurrent outcrossing across well-sampled nominal selfers would support it.

For hermaphrodites and candidate ancient asexuals, test genomes for meiosis genes, allele divergence, and the age of asexuality. The claim would be confirmed if every well-sampled lineage shows occasional outcrossing or a recent loss of sex. It would be refuted by a lineage that has persisted for many millions of years with no sex and no genomic sign of decline that an occasional cross would be needed to prevent.

obstacles: Darwin's phrase 'for an eternity of generations; perhaps at very long intervals' makes the timescale open-ended, requiring phylogenetic age estimation and genomic detection of rare historical recombination.
Distinguishing rare outcrossing from gene conversion or horizontal gene transfer in genomic data requires careful bioinformatic filtering.
An unlimited number of generations cannot be observed.
Rare outcrossing is difficult to exclude from finite genomic samples.
Rare sex, gene conversion, and horizontal transfer can mimic or mask long-term asexuality.
Many hermaphrodites still lack genomes dense enough for a Meselson-effect test.
Indispensable is a fitness claim that extant genomes record only indirectly.

claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.label: Land organisms change faster than marine organisms
claims.statement: Terrestrial organisms appear to change at a faster rate through geological time than marine organisms.

operationalizations.text: Compare median species and genus stratigraphic durations and per-million-year origination and extinction rates between terrestrial and marine clades in the fossil record.

Compare standardized origination, extinction, turnover, and morphological rates for matched terrestrial and marine clades and time bins. Support requires consistently higher rates on land after controlling for preservation, taxonomy, and clade composition.

Compare per-lineage origination, extinction, or morphological-change rates for terrestrial versus marine taxa over the same Phanerozoic intervals, after sampling standardization. Faster terrestrial change would support the claim; equal or slower terrestrial change would count against it.

obstacles: Terrestrial fossil preservation is much more episodic and spatially restricted than marine preservation, which truncates apparent stratigraphic ranges.
Differences in taxonomic splitting between terrestrial vertebrates/insects and marine invertebrates can bias rate comparisons.
Terrestrial preservation and sampling are much poorer than marine preservation.
'Change' can mean turnover or morphological evolution.
Land fossils are rarer and more episodic than marine shells, which moves apparent rates even when biological rates are similar.
Environment is incompletely coded, and many important terrestrial groups have little pre-Cenozoic record.

claims.label: Slow accumulated change hides the wild parents of old cultivated plants
claims.statement: Because a large amount of change has been slowly and unconsciously accumulated in long-cultivated plants, in many cases their wild parent-stocks can no longer be recognised.

operationalizations.text: Compare morphological distance vs genomic divergence between long-cultivated crops (e.g., maize, brassicas, cucurbits) and their wild relatives; test whether morphological divergence is so large that classical taxonomic/phenotypic clustering fails to identify the wild progenitor that genomic phylogenetics reveals.

Across long-cultivated plants, relate genomic and morphological divergence from inferred wild relatives to whether parent stocks were historically recognizable, controlling extinction and sampling. Greater accumulated change associated with failed recognition supports the explanation.

For plants with the longest cultivation histories, score whether a wild progenitor is identified and measure genomic or phenotypic distance to the nearest wild relative. The explanatory claim would be supported if unidentified progenitors were exactly the most diverged stocks; it would be weakened if large divergence still left progenitors identifiable, or if unidentified parents were mostly extinct or unsampled rather than unrecognizably modified.

obstacles: In some cases wild progenitors are unrecognized not because of extreme morphological divergence, but because the wild population went extinct or hybridized extensively.
Modern genomics can identify parents once unrecognizable morphologically.
Extinction and unsampled wild diversity are rival explanations.
A wild parent may be unrecognizable because it is extinct or uncollected, not because the crop changed.
Hybrid origins create several partial parents rather than one unrecognizable stock.
Minor garden plants are far less completely linked to wild relatives than major staples.

claims.label: Geometrical increase explains rapid spread of naturalised species
claims.statement: The extraordinarily rapid increase and wide spread of introduced (naturalised) animals and plants in new countries is explained by geometrical increase under favourable conditions with reduced mortality, not by any rise in their fertility.

operationalizations.text: Compare demographic vital rates (per-capita fecundity/seed output vs juvenile survival and enemy release) of invasive/naturalised plant and animal species between their native and introduced ranges using paired demographic datasets.

For dated introductions, fit spread and abundance trajectories using intrinsic growth, fertility in native versus introduced ranges, and stage-specific mortality. Rapid spread explained by reduced mortality without increased fertility supports the claim.

Compare fecundity of species in native versus introduced ranges, and compare survival or population growth over the same contrast, for naturalized plants and animals. Rapid spread with unchanged fecundity and higher survival would support geometrical increase under lower mortality; a systematic rise in fertility sufficient to explain the increase would count against the stated mechanism.

obstacles: In some invasive plants, reduced herbivory allows larger adult plant size, which increases total seed output per plant even if intrinsic physiological fertility is unchanged.
A specific dataset URL may not encode abundance or demography.
Introduction dates and early absences are uncertain.
Enemy release, adaptation and propagule pressure are confounded.
Vital-rate comparisons in both ranges exist for far fewer species than naturalization records.
Evolved increases in fecundity and enemy-release effects on body size can raise fertility after introduction.
GloNAF covers plants, while the statement also includes animals.

claims.label: Fertility of crossed varieties is not universal nor a species criterion
claims.statement: The fertility of varieties when crossed is very general but cannot be shown to be universal, so it does not form a fundamental distinction between varieties and species; some varieties, such as certain maize and Verbascum varieties, are partly sterile together.

operationalizations.text: Test for the existence of statistically significant prezygotic cross-incompatibility (e.g., gametophytic incompatibility factors such as $Ga1$ in Zea mays) or postzygotic hybrid sterility/lethality among recognized conspecific varieties, ecotypes, or subspecies in plants and animals.

Compare fertility of crosses among named varieties with within-variety controls and identify any reproducible partial sterility. A single robust counterexample refutes universality; prevalence estimates test 'very general.'

Compare the distribution of cross-fertility among named varieties with that among named species. Overlap, including partly sterile variety crosses such as maize lines, supports the denial of a universal fertility of varieties and of a fundamental fertility criterion; completely non-overlapping distributions would refute that denial.

obstacles: As Darwin noted, if taxonomists reclassify any partially sterile varieties as distinct species solely because of their sterility, the test becomes circular; using independent genomic/taxonomic classifications avoids this.
Variety definitions differ among studies.
Crossing failures are less likely to be published or deposited.
Varieties have often been ranked as varieties because they interbreed, which circularizes the contrast.
Maize and flies do not represent natural and domestic varieties generally.
Partial sterility in crops can be chromosomal engineering rather than the spontaneous case Darwin cited.

claims.label: Distinct southern genera spread from a once-vegetated Antarctica before the Glacial period
claims.statement: Distinct species of genera confined to the southern hemisphere spread in radiating lines from the antarctic lands, which supported a peculiar flora during a warmer period before the Glacial period, reaching southern America, Australia and New Zealand by occasional transport and former islands.

operationalizations.text: Examine pre-glacial (Cretaceous to Eocene/Oligocene) fossil pollen and macrofossils from Antarctica for southern-hemisphere disjunct genera (e.g., Nothofagus, Araucariaceae, Proteaceae, Podocarpaceae), and use dated molecular phylogenies to test whether divergences among South American, Australian, and New Zealand species reflect trans-Antarctic ancestral ranges and over-water dispersal.

For southern disjunct plant genera, infer ancestral areas and divergence dates and compare them with Antarctic fossils, paleoclimate, and changing island connections. Support requires Antarctic ancestry during a warm preglacial interval followed by outward lineage splits.

Combine pre-glacial Antarctic fossil plants with phylogenies of southern-hemisphere disjunct genera and ask whether those genera connect through an Antarctic source older than the glacial period. Roots centered only on Australia or South America, with no Antarctic fossil link, would count against the claim.

obstacles: Southern-hemisphere disjunctions reflect a combination of Gondwanan continental vicariance (which Darwin did not know) and post-breakup trans-oceanic dispersal via a vegetated Paleogene Antarctica.
Antarctic terrestrial fossil sampling is sparse.
Vicariance can mimic radiating dispersal.
Divergence estimates may not identify former stepping-stone islands.
The Antarctic macrofossil flora is small and geographically narrow.
Continental breakup, later dispersal, and an Antarctic source are hard to separate when divergence dates are uncertain.

claims.label: Some sterility in crosses between species is very general but not universal
claims.statement: Some degree of sterility in first crosses between species and in their hybrids is an extremely general result, but it is not absolutely universal.

operationalizations.text: Calculate the distribution of prezygotic crossability and postzygotic F1 hybrid fertility indices across large multi-taxon compilations of interspecific crosses in plants and animals; confirm if the vast majority show reduced fertility ($< 1.0$ relative to conspecific crosses) while a non-zero fraction of recognized species pairs produce fully fertile F1 hybrids.

Compile attempted interspecific crosses and estimate the frequency and degree of reduced F1 production and F1 fertility relative to within-species controls. High but non-unit prevalence supports the claim.

Estimate the proportion of interspecific crosses with reduced fertility of the first cross or the hybrids, and ask whether any well-documented crosses are fully fertile. A high proportion plus at least some fully fertile exceptions would support 'extremely general but not universal'; either rarity of sterility or no fertile exceptions would count against that wording.

obstacles: Taxonomic circularity can arise if taxonomists use reproductive isolation itself to delimit species, though phylogenetic and morphological species definitions allow independent tests.
Failed and null crosses are underreported.
Available crosses are a highly selected taxonomic sample.
Published crosses favor tractable taxa and both unusually fertile and unusually sterile outcomes.
Drosophila does not stand in for plants and animals at large.
Taxonomic rank affects the denominator of 'between species'.

claims.label: Cuckoo brood parasitism evolved from occasional laying in other birds’ nests
claims.statement: The brood-parasitic instinct of the European cuckoo was generated by natural selection from an ancestor that built its own nest but occasionally laid eggs in other birds’ nests, where the fostered young fared better.

operationalizations.text: Reconstruct the ancestral state of parental care vs. facultative and obligate brood parasitism across a time-calibrated phylogeny of Cuculidae (and other avian clades with brood parasites), and test whether obligate brood parasitism evolved from nest-building ancestors via facultative conspecific/interspecific parasitism and whether parasitic eggs/chicks achieve high fledging success in host nests.

Map nest building, facultative egg dumping, and obligate brood parasitism across a cuckoo phylogeny, reconstruct ancestral states, and compare offspring success. The predicted ordered transition and fitness advantage support the claim.

Reconstruct nest-building versus facultative and obligate brood parasitism on a cuckoo phylogeny, and repeat for cowbirds and honeyguides. A derived obligate state with nesting or facultative ancestors supports the sequence; parasitism ancestral to the family, or no intermediate state where sampling is good, would count against it.

obstacles: In Cuculidae, obligate parasitism evolved three independent times from nest-building ancestors, and extant intermediate facultative parasites (such as Coccyzus) are fewer than fully nest-building or obligate clades.
Behaviour and reproductive-success data are dispersed across studies.
Ancestral states are model-dependent.
Parasitic status and nesting behavior are not columns in these tree repositories and must be coded from monographs.
The selective claim that fostered young fared better is not in phylogenetic presence-absence data.
Extinct intermediates and hosts leave no behavioral fossils.

claims.label: Congeners compete more severely than species of different genera
claims.statement: Because species of the same genus are usually similar in habits and constitution and always in structure, competition between them is generally more severe than between species of different genera.

operationalizations.text: Test whether the strength of interspecific competition (pairwise competition coefficient α_ij, biomass suppression in common gardens, or niche overlap) is significantly higher between congeneric species than between heterogeneric species, or negatively correlated with phylogenetic distance.

Across competition experiments, compare interaction coefficients for congeneric species pairs with matched noncongeneric pairs, controlling functional similarity, environment and phylogenetic distance. Stronger average congeneric suppression supports the claim.

Compare competition coefficients, or naturalization and co-occurrence outcomes, for congeners versus species in different genera, controlling for habitat overlap. Stronger negative effects among congeners would support the statement; equal or weaker congener effects would refute it.

obstacles: Phylogenetic distance does not always map linearly onto functional niche similarity when convergent evolution or rapid adaptive divergence occurs within a genus.
Published interaction datasets are biased toward strong effects.
Congeneric status conflates relatedness with niche similarity.
Relatedness is an imperfect proxy for similarity of habits, so genus rank can miss the real competitors.
Habitat filtering makes close relatives co-occur, which looks like weak competition.
Experimental competition coefficients between congeners are far fewer than co-occurrence records.

claims.label: Domesticated forms vary more among individuals than wild species do
claims.statement: Individuals of the same variety of long-cultivated plants and domesticated animals generally differ much more from each other than individuals of any one species or variety in nature.

operationalizations.text: Compare within-variety/within-breed phenotypic coefficients of variation (CV) of morphological and physiological traits in domesticated animals and long-cultivated crops against within-species CVs of their wild progenitors or wild congeners.

Compare within-population phenotypic or genomic variance in matched domesticated and wild taxa using common trait scales and hierarchical models. Greater variance across most matched pairs supports the generalization; equal or lower domestic variance refutes it.

Compare within-variety coefficients of variation, or genomic heterozygosity, for homologous characters in long-cultivated populations and in wild populations of the parent species. Greater within-group dispersion in the domestic samples would support the contrast; equal or smaller domestic dispersion across a pre-registered trait set would refute it.

obstacles: Modern elite inbred crop lines and purebred livestock breeds have been artificially bred for extreme within-variety uniformity, whereas traditional landraces are more variable.
Sampling environments differ between farm/garden trials and wild field collections.
Management populations and wild populations are not sampled comparably.
Trait choice strongly affects variance.
Modern breed standards have deliberately reduced within-breed differences since the nineteenth century.
Genetic heterozygosity and visible individual differences can move in opposite directions after a domestication bottleneck.
Individual-level phenotypic measurements are scattered, while public sequence archives over-represent a few commercial species.
